newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition worries protests could fade.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition worries protests could fade.

text.p: Leaders of Serbia's two-month-long pro-democracy protests urged supporters to return in strength on Thursday following a relatively low turnout for the first rally after the Orthodox New Year.

"I hope I'll see double this number tomorrow and double that number the following day," Vuk Draskovic, a leader of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition, said to some 20,000 to 30,000 people demonstrating on Wednesday in central Belgrade.

The coalition is accustomed to having 100,000 or more for its daily protests to force President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialist government to reinstate annulled November 17 municipal elections in which the opposition won 14 of Serbia's 18 biggest cities.

The movement reached its peak on Orthodox New Year's Eve on Monday night when up to half a million people jammed the city centre, but the numbers were down sharply on Wednesday, the 59th day of protests across Serbia.

The opposition and student allies both suffered rude shocks on Wednesday -- Zajedno when a Socialist hardliner said the party would appeal an electoral commission ruling restoring the opposition victory in Belgrade, and students when a university council rejected their demand to sack the university rector.
The same day, motorists blocked traffic in the city centre of Novi Sad, police prevented a protest walk by some 2,000 people in Leskovac and about 500 people turned out in Kikinda.

In Nis, Serbia's second city where an electoral commission has ordered the opposition victory be recognised, 15,000 people demonstrated and the mayor invited Zajedno representatives to a meeting on Thursday.

Draskovic and his Zajedno co-leaders Zoran Djindjic and Vesna Pesic planned to fly to Italy on Thursday evening at the invitation of the Italian government for consultations with Prime Minister Romano Prodi and Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini.
"We are going at the invitation of the Italian government and Italy is sending a special plane for us," Djindjic told Reuters.
Dini infuriated the opposition on a visit to Serbia in December when he said that a reinstatement of the November 17 election results "is not on the cards".
Italy has since warmly endorsed the findings of an Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) investigation which recommended that the opposition victories be reinstated.
The Zajedno coalition and students, who have been demonstration separately in support of the election demands and for removal of the rector, both suffered setbacks on Wednesday.

Branislav Ivkovic, chief of the Socialist Party's Belgrade branch throughout the crisis, told the independent newspaper Blic that his party would challenge the commission ruling restoring the Zajedno victory in Belgrade.
"If it's true, we will use all legal means (to overturn the decision)," said Ivkovic, who was removed from his post on Tuesday in an SPS shakeup but appeared to remain influential.

Several thousand students waiting outside the university rectorate were stunned to learn that one of their principal demands, the sacking of rector Dragutin Velickovic, had been rejected by the university council.
The noisy crowd of students had waited all day for Velickovic to emerge but when Education Minister Dragoslav Mladenovic came out they chased him instead.
With the aid of security guards, Mladenovic took refuge in a nearby headquarters building of the Socialist Party.
